text: Eintracht Frankfurt e.V., based in Frankfurt, Hesse, is a German professional sports club founded on 8 March 1899. Its football club, established as Frankfurter Fußball-Club Victoria von 1899 and Frankfurter Fußball-Club Kickers von 1899, merged in May 1911 to form Frankfurter Fußball Verein (Kickers-Victoria), which later joined the gymnastics club Frankfurter Turngemeinde von 1861 in 1920 to create TuS Eintracht Frankfurt von 1861. The name "Eintracht" means 'harmony' or 'concord' and is equivalent to 'United' in English. In 1927, due to pressure from nationalistic gymnastics authorities, the football and gymnastics sections separated. The club has spent a total of 56 seasons in the top division of German football, making it the seventh longest continuously participating club in the Bundesliga. Eintracht is currently in the Bundesliga, the top tier of the German football league system, and has won the German championship once, the DFB-Pokal five times, the UEFA Europa League twice, and finished as runners-up in the European Cup once. It was one of the founding members of the Bundesliga in 1963 and played in the top division for 33 consecutive seasons, finishing in the top half of the table in most of those years. The club has 155,000 members, making it the fourth largest football club in Germany. Since 1925, the club has played at the Waldstadion, currently known as Deutsche Bank Park due to sponsorship. Eintracht has won or drawn more than three-quarters of their games and finished in the top half of the table in most seasons, despite having the highest number of losses in the league (657). With an average attendance of 47,942 since 2013, the club ranks eighth among the 36 Bundesliga and 2. Bundesliga teams for attendance. Charly Körbel, who made 602 appearances in the Bundesliga, spent his entire senior career as a defender with the club. The primary rival is Kickers Offenbach, though the two have only played two league matches in the last 40 years. In 2024, Eintracht Frankfurt has nearly 14,000 active athletes across over 50 sports, making it the largest multi-sports club in the world with a professional football team. The club won its first German championship in 1959, defeating rivals Kickers Offenbach 5–3 after extra time in front of 75,000 fans at Berlin's Olympiastadion. This victory earned them a place in the 1959–60 European Cup, where they defeated BSC Young Boys and Wiener Sport-Club to reach the semi-finals, winning 6–1 at home and 12–4 on aggregate against Rangers, who gave them a guard of honour. They lost 7–3 to Real Madrid in the final at Hampden Park, a match remembered for a hat-trick by Alfredo Di Stéfano and four goals by Ferenc Puskás. After 1959, Eintracht finished as runners-up in 1961 and 1962 in the Oberliga, missing the final both times. From 1973 to 1981, the club achieved its most successful period in the Bundesliga era, winning three DFB-Pokals and the UEFA Cup. The first DFB-Pokal title came in 1973–74, defeating Hamburger SV 3–1, with the final delayed until August 1974 due to the 1974 FIFA World Cup. They won again in 1975, beating MSV Duisburg 1–0, and reached the semi-finals of the European Cup Winners' Cup in 1975–76. Under coach Gyula Lóránt, Eintracht went unbeaten in the second half of the 1976–77 season, finishing fourth, only two points behind champions Borussia Mönchengladbach. Lóránt left for Bayern Munich, and Dettmar Cramer took over before being replaced by Otto Knefler, who left due to health issues. In January 1979, Friedel Rausch became head coach, and Cha Bum-kun joined in July, becoming the first Korean to play in Europe, scoring 12 goals in his debut season. Eintracht reached the UEFA Cup semi-finals, defeating Aberdeen, Dinamo București, Feyenoord, and FC Zbrojovka Brno, before being drawn against Bayern Munich and winning 5–1 in extra time. In the final, they lost 3–2 in the first leg to Borussia Mönchengladbach, but won on away goals after teenager Fred Schaub scored the decisive goal in the return leg. After Lothar Buchmann succeeded Rausch, Eintracht won their third DFB-Pokal in 1981, marking the end of their golden era. In 1984, they avoided relegation by defeating MSV Duisburg 6–1 on aggregate after finishing 16th. In 1986 and 1987, they finished 15th. In 1987–88, they finished in the top half of the league for the first time since 1982 and won the DFB-Pokal 1–0 over VfL Bochum, with Hungarian Lajos Détári scoring the goal; he was sold to Olympiacos two days later. In 1988–89, Jörg Berger led them to safety in a 4–1 aggregate win over 1. FC Saarbrücken in the relegation playoff. In 1990, Berger took the club to third place and was recognized as the best coach in the league. He left in 1991 after a fourth-place finish, but the squad included top Bundesliga players such as Uwe Bein, Uli Stein, Jørn Andersen, Manfred Binz, Tony Yeboah, and Andreas Möller. Dragoslav Stepanović took over and led the team to third place in both seasons, with his tenure considered one of the best in Bundesliga history. In 1991–92, Eintracht came close to winning the Bundesliga, leading the table until the final match, when they lost 2–1 after a disputed penalty decision, allowing VfB Stuttgart to win the title. In 1993–94, they led the table at halftime but fell to fifth place and Klaus Toppmöller was sacked. In 1994, Jupp Heynckes was appointed coach, but fell out with key players Tony Yeboah, Maurizio Gaudino, and Jay-Jay Okocha, leading to suspensions and departures; Heynckes left after the club finished 13th. Relegation occurred in 1995–96, ending 33 consecutive Bundesliga seasons, alongside 1. FC Kaiserslautern. After a difficult debut in the 2. Bundesliga, Eintracht won the title in 1997–98 and returned to the Bundesliga. Promotion coach Horst Ehrmantraut left in December, and Jörg Berger returned, saving the club on the final day of the 1998–99 season with a 5–1 win over Kaiserslautern due to a late goal by Jan Åge Fjørtoft. In 1999, the club was docked two points for license violations and survived on the last day of the season by beating SSV Ulm, who were relegated. In 2000, the club was relegated under Friedel Rausch and failed to return in 2001–02. Eintracht secured a Bundesliga return on the final day of the 2002–03 season with a 6–3 win over Reutlingen, scoring three goals in the last 10 minutes. They were immediately relegated back to the 2. Bundesliga but were promoted the following season under Friedhelm Funkel, who also led them to the DFB-Pokal final in 2005–06, losing to Bayern Munich. This also earned them a spot in the UEFA Cup. After years of stability, Michael Skibbe replaced Funkel in 2009. In 2010–11, the club suffered its fourth Bundesliga relegation after setting a record for most points in the first half of the season, then going seven games without scoring a goal. Coach Skibbe was replaced by Christoph Daum, but the club was relegated again after winning only once in the second half. In 2011–12, Eintracht defeated Alemannia Aachen 3–0 on the 32nd matchday to secure promotion. In 2012–13, they finished sixth in the Bundesliga, qualifying for the Europa League. In 2014–15, they finished in the top half of the league, with Alexander Meier as the league's top scorer. In 2015–16, they struggled and Niko Kovač was appointed in March 2016. They survived through the relegation playoff, finishing 16th and beating 1. FC Nürnberg 2–1 on aggregate. In Kovač's first full season, they survived comfortably and reached the 2017 DFB-Pokal final, losing to Borussia Dortmund. In 2017–18, they reached their second DFB-Pokal final in a row, winning 3–1 against heavy favourites Bayern Munich, despite Kovač agreeing to join the club the following season. He was replaced by Adi Hütter. In 2018–19, the attacking trio of Luka Jović, Ante Rebić, and Sébastien Haller scored 41 league goals and 16 Europa League goals, receiving widespread praise.

During the 2014–15 season, Eintracht Frankfurt's Alexander Meier was the league's top scorer, but the team struggled in 2015–16, finishing 16th and surviving only through a relegation playoff, where they defeated 1. FC Nürnberg 2–1 on aggregate. Niko Kovač was appointed coach in March 2016, and in his first full season, the team survived comfortably and reached the 2017 DFB-Pokal final, losing to Borussia Dortmund. In 2017–18, Eintracht reached their second consecutive DFB-Pokal final, winning 3–1 against heavy favourites Bayern Munich—Kovač had already agreed to join Bayern from the next season—and he was replaced by Adi Hütter. In 2018–19, Luka Jović, Ante Rebić, and Sébastien Haller formed an attacking trio that scored 41 league goals and 16 Europa League goals, earning the nickname "the Buffalo Herd," and Eintracht won all six group games in the Europa League against Lazio, Apollon Limassol, Marseille, Shakhtar Donetsk, Inter Milan, and Benfica, drawing both legs 1–1 in the semi-finals against Chelsea before losing on penalties at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea won the tournament, and Eintracht missed Champions League qualification after dropping from 4th to 7th. After Jović, Rebić, and Haller left in summer 2019, the team regressed in 2019–20 and failed to qualify for Europe, but returned to the Europa League with a 5th-place finish in 2020–21, after which Adi Hütter left for Borussia Mönchengladbach. In the 2021–22 Europa League, Eintracht topped their group, stunned Barcelona in the quarter-finals with a 3–0 lead at Camp Nou and won 3–2, with approximately 30,000 Frankfurt fans in attendance, and beat West Ham home and away in the semi-finals to reach their first European final since 1980. In the final at Seville's Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán Stadium, Frankfurt beat Rangers 5–4 on penalties after a 1–1 draw in extra-time, with Rafael Santos Borré scoring Eintracht's goal and the winning penalty; goalkeeper Kevin Trapp was named man of the match after making a crucial late save from Ryan Kent and saving Aaron Ramsey's penalty. Eintracht won the competition unbeaten, qualifying for the 2022–23 UEFA Champions League, their first appearance since 1960; they finished second in their group and advanced to the knockout stages, but lost in the round of 16 to S.S.C. Napoli. In the 2022–23 DFB-Pokal, the team reached the final on 3 June 2023, losing 2–0 to RB Leipzig, and a 7th-place finish secured qualification for the UEFA Europa Conference League. Since November 2024, the executive board consists of Axel Hellmann (CEO), Markus Krösche (head of sports), Julien Zamberk (head of finances), and Philipp Reschke (head of fan relations, merchandising and HR). The club crest originates from the coat of arms of Frankfurt, referencing the 13th-century one-headed Imperial Eagle, and evolved with little change until 1980, when a stylized black and white eagle was adopted; in 1999, during its centenary, the club re-adopted a more traditional eagle crest. Since 2005, Eintracht has had a living mascot, a golden eagle named Attila from the Hanau Zoo, who has been present at over 200 games. The official club colours—red, black, and white—come from the founding clubs Frankfurter FC Viktoria (red and white) and Frankfurter FC Kickers (black and white); red and white are from the city coat of arms, and black and white from Prussia. After the merger, both sets of colours were adopted, and since Kickers Offenbach wear red and white, Eintracht avoids that kit, preferring black and red or black and white; in the 2023–2024 season, the home kit is black and red. In the 2021–22 Europa League, Eintracht played an unbeaten campaign with an all-white kit, earning the nickname "la bestia blanca" (the white beast), a play on "la bestia negra" (the black beast), after knocking out Barcelona. The club is nicknamed "Die Adler" (The Eagles), derived from the logo, and supporters also use "SGE," from the old name Sportgemeinde Eintracht (Frankfurt), meaning "Sports Community Harmony." The nickname "Launische Diva" (Moody Diva) was common in the early 1990s when Eintracht defeated top teams but lost to weaker ones. "Schlappekicker" (Slipper Kickers) dates back to the 1920s, when J. & C. A. Schneider, a local slipper manufacturer, was a major backer. Green denotes the highest level of German football; yellow the second. The club's initial games from 1899 to 1906 were played on the former Hundswiese field, near Hessischer Rundfunk; in 1906, they established Victoriaplatz by Eschersheimer Landstraße, purchasing stands for 350 marks in 1908; from 1912, they moved to Roseggerstraße in Dornbusch, then to the former Riederwaldstadion in 1920 after merging with Frankfurter Turngemeinde von 1861. The stadium was inaugurated as Waldstadion in 1925 with the German championship final between FSV Frankfurt and 1. FC Nürnberg; it was renovated for the 2006 FIFA World Cup and has a maximum capacity of 59,500 for Bundesliga fixtures as of 2025. Though officially called Deutsche Bank Park, fans typically refer to it as Waldstadion. Eintracht Frankfurt U21 is the reserve team, previously known as U23 to emphasize its role as a youth-pro to professional link; the club dissolved the team after the 2013–14 season in the Regionalliga Süd. On 14 February 2022, the club applied to re-admit the reserves to the Hessenliga for the 2022–23 season, and in their first season back, Frankfurt II won the Hessenliga and was promoted to the Regionalliga Südwest, where they now play. The main rival is Kickers Offenbach, across the Main River, with the two clubs having played in the 1959 German championship final, which Eintracht won. Eintracht also has regional rivalries with Darmstadt 98 (Hesse derby) and with 1. FSV Mainz 05 and 1. FC Kaiserslautern in Rhineland-Palatinate. The original rival was FSV Frankfurt, with a fierce early rivalry that faded after World War II due to Eintracht's dominance and lack of contact; today, fan relations are generally friendly. In the 2011–12 season, Eintracht played FSV in a league match for the first time in nearly 50 years—the last being on 27 January 1962 in the Oberliga Süd—first on 21 August 2011 at Eintracht's stadium (due to FSV's Bornheimer Hang holding fewer than 11,000), which ended 4–0, and again on 18 February 2012, which ended 6–1. A friendship between Eintracht fan clubs and Oldham Athletic supporters has lasted over 30 years, with small sections visiting each other's grounds at least once a season. Eintracht also has an international friendship with Atalanta supporters. The sports club Eintracht Frankfurt e.V. has nineteen sections, including athletics, where Betty Heidler (2007 hammer throw world champion) and Olympians Andrea Bunjes, Ariane Friedrich, Kamghe Gaba, and Kathrin Klaas were members; the rugby union section reached the German championship final twice, in 1940 and 1965. Within football, the club directly manages only the youth system and the reserve team; professional footballers are managed by Eintracht Frankfurt Fußball-AG, a subsidiary of the parent club.
